title: The Phish the Model Was Sure Was Fine
input_data:
Email metadata for a message in the finance team inbox:

Subject: New contractor payment schedule - urgent
From: vendors@synapse-group.co (external, domain registered 3 days ago)
Reply-to: payables-synapse@gmail.com (personal free mailbox)
Body: 'Update your banking details by 5pm today or your invoice payments are paused. Login at the link to confirm.'
Attachment: invoice_0912.xlsm (macro-enabled)
The sender is not a known vendor. Finance staff routinely receive payment emails, so this looks similar to thousands of legitimate ones.
ai_output: Low risk. The message closely matches the common 'payment reminder' template in the training data. Likely benign vendor communication. No action required.
ground_truth: Targeted phishing attack. The message is a spear phish aimed at the finance team: a fake vendor, a freshly registered domain, a personal mailbox as reply target, and a macro-enabled attachment. The model missed it because its training set contained almost no attacks (99.9% benign email), so the safest prediction in its learned distribution was always 'benign'.
explanation: The training data was dominated by benign examples, so the model learned that predicting 'benign' is almost always right. Class imbalance biases the model toward the majority class; the rare, important class (attack) is under-learned and systematically missed, even when the evidence is strong.
security_impact: The phishing email reaches a finance user who, trusting the system's 'benign' label, clicks the macro and enters credentials on the fake login page. The attack succeeds because the detection tool certified it as safe.
recommended_validation: Never treat a majority-class prediction as proof. Score phishing risk on independent signals such as domain age, reply-to mismatch, attachment type, and urgency pressure, and validate the model on a balanced test set that includes real attack samples.

possible_mitigations.name: Balanced evaluation sets
possible_mitigations.description: Evaluate the model on a test set with real attack samples so misses on the rare class are visible and counted.

possible_mitigations.name: Signal-based phishing scoring
possible_mitigations.description: Score messages on concrete indicators such as domain age, reply-to mismatch, and macro attachments instead of template similarity alone.

possible_mitigations.name: False negative monitoring
possible_mitigations.description: Track reported phishing that was previously labeled benign and feed those cases back as training signal.

possible_mitigations.name: Human review of edge cases
possible_mitigations.description: Route messages that are close to the benign template but carry risk indicators to an analyst for review.

learning_objective: Class imbalance biases a model toward the majority class. In security the rare class is usually the one that matters, and a balanced test set is required to see how badly it is missed.
teaching_points: When 99.9% of training data is benign, the model learns to say benign.
The rare class, an attack, is exactly what a security tool must catch.
Validate on balanced sets and score signals, not template similarity.
